title: Where glucose splitting starts
q: In a typical eukaryotic cell, where does glycolysis occur?
why: Glycolysis occurs in the cytosol, outside the mitochondrion. Its products can enter further pathways depending on conditions.

title: Pyruvate enters the organelle
q: In a typical eukaryotic cell, where does pyruvate oxidation to acetyl-CoA occur?
why: In eukaryotic cells, pyruvate oxidation occurs in the mitochondrial matrix, where acetyl-CoA can enter the citric acid cycle.

title: The citric acid cycle's home
q: In a typical eukaryotic cell, where do most citric acid cycle reactions occur?
why: Most citric acid cycle reactions occur in the mitochondrial matrix. One enzyme, succinate dehydrogenase, is embedded in the inner membrane.

title: A chain in a folded boundary
q: In mitochondria, where are the major electron-transport-chain complexes embedded?
why: The mitochondrial electron-transport complexes are embedded in the inner membrane. The membrane folds, called cristae, increase its surface area.

title: The ATP-making channel
q: In mitochondria, which boundary contains ATP synthase for oxidative phosphorylation?
why: Mitochondrial ATP synthase is embedded in the inner membrane. Proton flow through it helps drive ATP synthesis.

title: A proton gradient builds
q: During mitochondrial electron transport, protons are pumped from the matrix into which compartment?
why: The chain pumps protons across the inner membrane from the matrix to the intermembrane space, contributing to an electrochemical gradient.

title: A proton gradient is used
q: During mitochondrial ATP synthesis, protons flow through ATP synthase from the intermembrane space toward which compartment?
why: Protons flow down their electrochemical gradient through ATP synthase toward the mitochondrial matrix, helping drive ATP formation.

title: Oxygen at the end of the chain
q: Where is the mitochondrial respiratory chain that transfers electrons to oxygen at its end?
why: The respiratory chain is in the inner mitochondrial membrane. At its end, oxygen accepts electrons and combines with protons to form water.

title: Where light reactions happen
q: In a chloroplast, where are the main light-dependent photosynthetic reaction complexes located?
why: The light-dependent photosynthetic complexes are embedded in thylakoid membranes. The diagram shows simplified stacks, not individual protein complexes.

title: Where carbon is fixed
q: In a chloroplast, where do the Calvin cycle reactions take place?
why: The Calvin cycle takes place in the stroma, the fluid space surrounding the thylakoids. It uses ATP and NADPH produced by the light reactions.

title: The carbon-fixing enzyme
q: In a chloroplast, where does the Calvin-cycle enzyme RuBisCO fix carbon dioxide?
why: RuBisCO participates in carbon fixation in the chloroplast stroma. The simplified diagram shows the compartment, not individual enzymes.

title: A second proton gradient
q: During chloroplast light reactions, protons accumulate inside which compartment of the thylakoid?
why: Light-driven electron transport and water splitting contribute to proton accumulation in the thylakoid lumen. The gradient can then help power ATP synthesis.

title: A channel in a green organelle
q: In chloroplasts, where is the ATP synthase that uses the light-driven proton gradient embedded?
why: Chloroplast ATP synthase is embedded in the thylakoid membrane. Proton movement through it helps drive ATP formation.

title: Protons flow back through
q: During chloroplast ATP synthesis, protons flow through ATP synthase from the thylakoid lumen toward which compartment?
why: Protons flow through ATP synthase from the thylakoid lumen toward the stroma, helping drive ATP synthesis.

title: Water supplies electrons
q: Where is photosystem II, the complex that obtains electrons by splitting water, embedded?
why: Photosystem II is embedded in the thylakoid membrane. Water splitting supplies electrons and releases oxygen and protons.
